---
title: "Files"
---

## miniSEED

```python
load("data/acq.mseed")                                   # one signal per channel: S1, S2...
load("data/acq.mseed", select="*.*.*.FH?", unit="V", sensitivity=2.384e-6)
load("data/acq.mseed", starttime="2026-11-17T10:00:00", endtime="2026-11-17T11:00:00")
load("data/acq.mseed", gaps="fill")
```

`/load data/acq.mseed unit=V sensitivity=2.384e-6` does the same in the console.

A miniSEED file is recognized by its content, whatever its name: the day files of an SDS
archive, named `NET.STA.LOC.CHA.TYPE.YEAR.DAY` (`XX.LORA.HA.BHE.D.2026.264`, day 264 of 2026)
have no `.mseed` extension and load as well. A day at 250 Hz is 21.6 million samples (about
170 MB in memory): it loads in about a second, and its long-period PSD (`lnm`) in about as
much.

**Gaps are never filled silently.** The `gaps` option chooses the policy:

| `gaps` | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `longest` (default) | keep the longest continuous segment |
| `fill` | fill by linear interpolation (do not measure noise on filled parts) |
| `split` | one signal per continuous segment |
| `error` | refuse the file |

Whatever the policy, the gaps are listed in `S.gaps`, shown by `S.print()` and recalled in
every result.

## Several days (SDS archives)

An SDS archive keeps one miniSEED file per channel and per day, named
`NET.STA.LOC.CHA.TYPE.YEAR.DAY`, usually in `<root>/YEAR/NET/STA/CHA.D/`. For a long-period
noise model (`lnm`), several days are loaded into one signal per channel:

```python
sds_channels("data/archive")      # channels found (first and last day, missing days, size)
load_sds("data/archive", "XX.LORA.HA.BHE", "2026-09-21", "2026-09-24")   # three days
load_sds("data/archive", "*.BH?", "2026-09-21T06:00", "2026-09-21T12:00")  # several channels
load("data/uploads/XX.LORA.HA.BHE.D.2026.2*")      # a pattern (or a list) of files, merged
```

The folder is searched for these names whatever its layout: day files copied or uploaded into
one folder are found as well. `starttime` and `endtime` limit the records read (a day file may
end a few seconds after midnight: the file of the neighbouring day is read too when the window
comes near midnight). A missing day is a gap, handled by `gaps` as for one file: `longest`
keeps the longest continuous segment, `split` gives one signal per continuous segment. The
title spans the days of each signal (`XX.LORA.HA.BHE.D.2026.264-266`); its SHA-256 is the
digest of the names and digests of the files read.

In the console, `/sds data/archive` lists the channels and
`/sds data/archive XX.LORA.HA.BHE 2026-09-21 2026-09-24 gaps=split` loads one. A day at
250 Hz is 21.6 million samples, about 170 MB in memory.

## Signal title

Every loaded signal gets a **title**: by default the file name without its extension
(`data/acquisition_FHZ.mseed` → `acquisition_FHZ`), or the whole name of a day file of an
SDS archive, whose last part is the day of the year (`XX.LORA.HA.BHE.D.2026.264`). All the channels of a file share it; the
NSLC code tells them apart. The title appears in:

- the title of every result and figure: `Noise — S1 · acquisition_FHZ (RD.SN270.00.FHZ) · …`;
- the `Title` column of `list_sig()` and of the "Analysed signals" table of reports;
- `S1.print()`, the AI context and the header of text/CSV exports.

Choose another title when loading, or change it at any time:

```python
load("data/acq.mseed", title="Bench test, gain 1")       # same title for every channel
load("bench.txt", n_channels=2, fs=1000, title=["X axis", "Y axis"])  # one per channel
S1.title = "Shorted input, 20 °C"
```

`/load data/acq.mseed title="Bench test"` does the same in the console. A signal derived from
another one (`2 * S1`, `S1.slice(...)`, `S1.filter(...)`) keeps its title; the sum or the
difference of two signals with different titles is titled `title1 + title2` or
`title1 − title2`. The miniSEED format cannot store the title: a re-loaded export is titled
after its new file name.

## Text files

One column per channel, with an optional time column. The number of channels is mandatory and
checked against the file.

```python
load("bench.txt", n_channels=3, fs=1000)                 # no time column
load("scope.csv", n_channels=2, time_col=0, decimal=",") # time in column 0, decimal comma
load("log.txt", n_channels=1, time_col=0, time_format="iso")
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `n_channels` | asked | number of data columns |
| `time_col` | none | index of the time column |
| `fs` | from the time column | sampling rate, mandatory without time column |
| `delimiter` | automatic | tab, `;`, `,` or spaces |
| `decimal` | `.` | `,` accepted |
| `skiprows`, `comment` | automatic, `#` | header lines |
| `time_format` | `relative` | `relative` (s), `epoch` or `iso` |
| `starttime` | 1970-01-01 | time origin for relative times |
| `names`, `units`, `sensitivities` | `XX.<file>..C01`… | per-channel codes and parameters |
| `title` | file name | signal title, one for all channels or one per channel |
| `resample` | false | interpolate an irregular time column instead of failing |

With a time column, the sampling rate is the inverse of the median step; a step deviating by
more than 1 % from it is an error (unless `resample=True`). In the console, `/load file.txt`
asks the number of channels, the time column and, when needed, the sampling rate.

## Export

```python
S1.save("S1.mseed")    # miniSEED, STEIM2 for integer counts (SEED code lengths checked)
S1.save("S1.csv")      # header (id, title, unit...) + time (s) and value (counts)
r.save("result.json")  # any result; .csv gives the table of values
```
